Martin Heidegger (
GA 7
) Early Greek Thinking

title: Early Greek Thinking 77
headings: Martin Heidegger ( GA 7 ) Early Greek Thinking
text:
Logos (Heraclitus, Fragment B 50)

 "To bring to language" usually means to express something
 orally or in writing. But the phrase now wishes to think something else:
 "to bring to language" means to secure Being in the essence of language.
 May we suggest that such an event prepared itself when d
 Λόγος became the guiding word of Heraclitus' thinking, because it
 became the name for the Being of beings?

 Ὁ Λόγος, τὸ Λέγειν, is the Laying that gathers. But at the same
 time λέγειν always means for the Greeks to lay before, to exhibit, to
 tell, to say. Ὁ Λόγος then would be the Greek name for speaking,
 saying, and language. Not only this. Ὁ Λόγος, thought as the Laying
 that gathers, would be the essence of saying [
die Sage
] as thought by
 the Greeks.
 {
GA 7: 232
}
 Language would be saying. Language would be the gathering
 letting-lie-before of what is present in its presencing. In fact, the
 Greeks dwelt in this essential determination of language. But they
 never thought it—Heraclitus included.

 The Greeks do experience saying in this way. But, Heraclitus
 included, they never think the essence of language expressly as the
 Λόγος, as the Laying that gathers.

 What would have come to pass had Heraclitus—and all the Greeks
 after him—thought the essence of language expressly as Λόγος, as the
 Laying that gathers! Nothing less than this: the Greeks would have
 thought the essence of language from the essence of Being—indeed, as
 this itself. For ὁ Λόγος is the name for the Being of beings. Yet none of
 this came to pass. Nowhere do we find a trace of the Greeks' having
 thought the essence of language directly from the essence of Being.
 Instead, language came to be represented—indeed first of all with the
 Greeks—as vocalization, φωνή, as sound and voice, hence phonetically.
 The Greek word that corresponds to our word "language" is
 γλῶσσα, "tongue." Language is φωνὴ σημαντική, a vocalization which
 signifies something. This suggests that language attains at the outset
 that preponderant character which we designate with the name "expression."
 This correct but externally contrived representation of language,
 language as "expression," remains definitive from now on. It is
 still so today. Language is taken to be expression, and vice versa.
 Every kind of expression is represented as a kind of language. Art
 historians speak of the "language of forms."

77

Martin Heidegger (
GA 7
) Early Greek Thinking

title: Early Greek Thinking 79
headings:
Moira 
 (Parmenides VIII, 34-41)
Martin Heidegger ( GA 7 ) Early Greek Thinking
text:
THREE

 Moira

 (Parmenides VIII, 34-41)

 The relation between thinking and Being animates all Western
 reflection. It remains the durable touchstone for determining to what
 extent and in what way we have been granted both the privilege and
 the capacity to approach that which addresses itself to historical man as
 to-be-thought. Parmenides names this relation in his saying (Frag. III):

 τὸ γὰρ αὐτὸ νοεῖν ἐστίν τε καὶ εἶναι.

 For thinking and Being are the same.

 In another verse, Fragment VIII, (34—41) he elaborates this saying. The
 lines read:

 ταὐτὸν δ' ἐστὶ νοεῖν τε καὶ οὕνεκεν ἔστι νόημα.

 οὐ γὰρ ἄνευ τοῦ ἐόντος, ἐν ᾧ πεφατισμένον ἐστιν,

 εὑρήσεις τὸ νοεῖν· οὐδὲν γὰρ ἢ ἔστιν ἢ ἔσται

 ἄλλο πάρεξ τοῦ ἐόντος, ἐπεὶ τό γε Μοῖρ' ἐπέδησεν

 οὖλον ἀκίνητόν τ' ἔμμεναι: τῷ πάντ' ὄνομ' ἔσται,

 ὅσσα βροτοὶ κατέθεντο πεποιθότες εἶναι ἀληθῆ,

 γίγνεσθαί τε καὶ ὄλλυσθαι, εἶναί τε καὶ οὐχί,

 καὶ τόπον ἀλλάσσειν διά τε χρόα φανὸν ἀμείβειν.

 Thinking and the thought "it is" are the same. For without the being in relation
 to which it is uttered you cannot find thinking. For there neither is nor shall be
 anything outside of being, since Moira bound it to be whole and immovable.
 For that reason, all these will be mere names which mortals have laid down,
 convinced that they were true: coming-to-be as well as passing away. Being as
 well as nonbeing, and also change of place and variation of shining colors.*

 *Cf. Diels-Kranz, 
Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker
, I, 238. Heidegger's citation of
 Fragment VIII differs from that of Diels-Kranz in two respects: he replaces the Greek
 semicolon (·) in lines 36 and 38 with a colon(:), and employs a variant spelling for ἔμεναι
 (1. 38). On the latter see below, p. 
91
—TR.

79

Martin Heidegger (
GA 7
) Early Greek Thinking

GA 7: 237

title: Early Greek Thinking 82
headings: Martin Heidegger ( GA 7 ) Moira (Parmenides VIII, 34-41)
text:
EARLY GREEK THINKING

 Modern philosophy experiences beings as objects [
Gegenstand
],
 It is through and for perception that the object comes to be a "standing
 against." As Leibniz clearly saw, 
percipere
 is like an appetite which
 seeks out the particular being and attacks it, in order to grasp it and
 wholly subsume it under a concept, relating this being's presence
 [
Präsenz
] back to the 
percipere (repraesentare). Repraesentatio
,
 representation [
Vorstellung
], is defined as the perceptive self-arrogation
 (to the self as ego) of what appears.

 Among the doctrines of modern philosophy there is one outstanding
 formulation which is unfailingly regarded as the final solution by all
 those who with the help of modern philosophy undertake to clarify
 Parmenides' saying. We mean Berkeley's proposition, which is based
 on the fundamental position of Descartes' metaphysics and says: esse =
 percipi, Being equals being represented. Being falls under the sway of
 representation, understood in the sense of perception. This proposition
 fashions the context in which the saying of Parmenides first becomes
 accessible to a scientific-philosophical explanation which removes
 it from that aura of half-poetical "presentiment" to which Presocratic
 thinking is usually consigned. 
Esse
 = 
percipi
. Being is being
 represented. It is by virtue of representing that Being is. Being is
 identical with thinking insofar as the objectivity of objects is composed
 and constituted in the representing consciousness, in the "I think
 something." In light of this assertion regarding the relation between
 Being and thinking, the saying of Parmenides comes to be viewed as a
 crude prefiguring of contemporary doctrines of reality and the knowledge
 of reality.

 It is no accident that Hegel, in his 
Lectures on the History of Philosophy

 (
Works
, 2d. ed., XIII, 274), translates and discusses this
 saying of Parmenides concerning the relation of Being and thinking:

 {
GA 7: 241
}

 "Thinking, and that for the sake of which there is thought, are the same. For
 without the beings in which it is expressed (ἐν ᾧ πεφοτασμένον ἐστιν) you will
 not find thinking; for thinking, without beings, is and shall be nothing." This is
 the main thought. Thinking produces itself, and what is produced is a thought.

82

Martin Heidegger (
GA 7
) Moira (Parmenides VIII, 34-41)

title: Early Greek Thinking 83
headings: Martin Heidegger ( GA 7 ) Early Greek Thinking
text:
Moira (Parmenides VIII, 34-41)

 Thinking is thus identical with its Being; for there is nothing outside of Being,
 this great affirmation.

 For Hegel Being is the affirmation of self-productive thought. Being is
 the product of thinking, of perception, in the sense in which Descartes
 had already interpreted 
idea
. Through thinking, Being as
 affirmation and as the positing of representation is transposed into the
 realm of the "ideal." For Hegel also—though in an incomparably more
 thoughtful way, a way mediated by Kant—Being is the same as thinking.
 It is the same as thinking in that Being is what is expressed and
 affirmed by thinking. Thus, from the standpoint of modern philosophy,
 Hegel can pass the following judgment upon the saying of Parmenides:

 In that this saying gives evidence of ascending into the realm of the ideal,
 genuine philosophizing began with Parmenides; this beginning is of
 course still dark and indefinite and does not further explain what is contained
 in it; but just this explanation constitutes the development of philosophy
 itself—which is not yet present here. (pp. 274 ff.)

 For Hegel philosophy is at hand only when the self-thinking of
 absolute knowledge is reality itself, and simply is. The self-perfecting
 elevation of Being into the thinking of Spirit as absolute reality takes
 place in and as speculative logic.

 On the horizon of this consummation of modern philosophy Parmenides'
 saying appears as the very beginning of genuine philosophizing,
 i.e. as the beginning of logic in Hegel's sense—but only as a
 beginning. Parmenides' thought lacks the speculative,
 {
GA 7: 242
}
 dialectical form
 which Hegel does however find in Heraclitus. Referring to Heraclitus
 Hegel says, "Here we see land; there is no sentence in Heraclitus
 which I have not taken up into my 
Logic
." Hegel's 
Logic
 is not only the
 one and only suitable interpretation of Berkeley's proposition in modern
 times; it is its unconditioned realization. That Berkeley's assertion

esse
 = 
percipi
 concerns precisely what Parmenides' saying first put into
 words has never been doubted. But this historical kinship of the modern
 proposition and the ancient saying at the same time has its proper
 foundation in a difference between what is said and thought in our
 times and what was said and thought at that time—a difference which
 could hardly be more decisive.

 The dissimilarity between the two is so far-reaching that through it
 the very possibility of comprehending the difference is shattered.

83

Martin Heidegger (
GA 7
) Early Greek Thinking

title: Early Greek Thinking 85
headings: Martin Heidegger ( GA 7 ) Early Greek Thinking
text:
Moira (Parmenides VIII, 34-41)

 Being belongs in
 the realm of the νοεῖν, the non- and supersensible. Plotinus interprets
 Parmenides' saying in the Platonic sense, according to which Parmenides
 wants to say: Being is something nonsensible. Here the emphasis
 of the saying falls on thinking, although not in the way this is
 understood in modern philosophy. Being is identified in terms of
 thinking's nonsensible nature. Interpreted from the Neoplatonic perspective,
 Parmenides' saying is an assertion neither about thinking nor
 about Being, nor even about the essential belonging-together of both in
 their difference. The saying is rather an assertion about the equal participation
 of both in the realm of the nonsensible.

 Each of these three viewpoints draws the early thinking of the
 Greeks into a region dominated by the spheres of questioning of subsequent
 metaphysics. Presumably, however, all later thinking which
 seeks dialogue with ancient thinking should listen continually from
 within its
 {
GA 7: 244
}
 own standpoint, and should thereby bring the silence of
 ancient thinking to expression. In this process, of course, the earlier
 thinking is inevitably accommodated to the later dialogue, into whose
 frame of reference and ways of hearing it is transposed. The earlier
 thinking is thus, as it were, deprived of its own freedom of speech. But
 this accommodation in no way restricts one to an interpretation completely
 dedicated to reinterpreting the to-be-thought at the beginning
 of Western thinking exclusively in terms of subsequent modes of representation.
 All depends on whether the dialogue we have undertaken
 first of all and continually allows itself to respond to the questioning
 address of early thinking, or whether it simply closes itself off to such
 an address and cloaks early thought with the mantle of more recent
 doctrines. This happens as soon as subsequent thinking neglects to

inquire properly
 into the ways of hearing and frames of reference of
 early thinking.

 An effort at proper inquiry should not end in a historical investigation
 which merely establishes the unexpressed presuppositions underlying
 early thought; that is, proper inquiry is not an investigation in
 which these presuppositions are taken into account solely with respect
 to whatever subsequent interpretation either validates as already posited
 truth or invalidates as having been superseded by further developments.

85

Martin Heidegger (
GA 7
) Early Greek Thinking

title: Early Greek Thinking 86
headings: Martin Heidegger ( GA 7 ) Moira (Parmenides VIII, 34-41)
text:
EARLY GREEK THINKING

 Unlike this type of investigation, proper inquiry must be a
 dialogue in which the ways of hearing and points of view of ancient
 thinking are contemplated according to their essential origin, so that
 the call [
Geheiss
] under which past, present, and future
 thinking—each in its own way—all stand, might begin to announce itself. An
 attempt at such inquiry should first direct its attention to the obscure
 passages of the ancient text, and should not settle upon those which
 give the appearance of easy intelligibility. To focus on the latter would
 end the dialogue before it has begun.

 The following discussion limits itself to working through the cited
 text by a series of individual commentaries. These may help to prepare
 a thoughtful translation of early Greek speech by advancing a thinking
 which is awake to beginnings.

 {
GA 7: 245
}

I

 The topic under discussion is the relation between thinking and
 Being. In the first place we ought to observe that the text (VIII, 34-41)
 which ponders this relation more thoroughly speaks of ἐόν and not—as
 in Fragment III—about εἶναι. Immediately, and with some justification,
 one concludes from this that Fragment VIII concerns beings
 rather than Being. But in saying ἐόν Parmenides is in no way thinking
 "beings in themselves," understood as the whole to which thinking,
 insofar as it is some kind of entity, also belongs. Just as little does ἐόν
 mean εἶναι in the sense of "Being for itself," as though it were incumbent
 upon the thinker to set the nonsensible essential nature of Being
 apart from, and in opposition to, beings which are sensible. Rather
 ἐόν, being, is thought here in its duality as Being and beings, and is
 participially expressed—although the grammatical concept has not yet
 come explicitly into the grasp of linguistic science. This duality is at
 least intimated by such nuances of phrasing as "the Being of beings"
 and "beings in Being." In its essence, however, what unfolds is obscured
 more than clarified through the "in" and the "of." These expressions
 are far from thinking the duality as such, or from seriously questioning
 its unfolding.

 "Being itself," so frequently invoked, is held to be true so long as
 it is experienced as Being, consistently understood as the Being of
 beings.

86

Martin Heidegger (
GA 7
) Moira (Parmenides VIII, 34-41)

title: Early Greek Thinking 89
headings: Martin Heidegger ( GA 7 ) Early Greek Thinking
text:
Moira (Parmenides VIII, 34-41)

 Simply through the fact that the duality on account of which mortals
 find themselves thinking, demands such thinking for itself.

 We are still far from experiencing the duality itself—that is, at the
 same time, so far as it demands thinking—far from experiencing it in an
 essential way. Only one thing is clear from the saying of Parmenides:
 neither on account of ἐόντα, "beings in themselves," nor for
 {
GA 7: 248
}
 the sake of
 εἶναι, "Being for itself," does thinking come to presence. That is to say:
 a "being in itself," does not make thinking mandatory, nor does "Being
 for itself' necessitate thought. Neither, taken separately, will ever let it
 be known to what extent "Being" calls for thinking. But because of
 their duality, because of the ἐόν, thinking comes to presence. The
 taking-heed of Being comes to presence on the way to the duality. In
 such a presencing thinking belongs to Being. What does Parmenides
 say about this belonging?

III

 Parmenides says that νοεῖν πεφατισμένον ἐν τῷ ἐόντι. This is
 translated: "thinking, which as something uttered is in being." But how
 can we ever hope to experience and understand this being-uttered so
 long as we do not take the trouble to question what "utterance," "to
 speak," and "language" mean here, or so long as we hastily accept ἐόν
 as a being and let the meaning of Being remain undetermined? How
 can we ever come to recognize the connection of νοεῖν to
 πεφατισμένον so long as we do not adequately determine the νοεῖν by
 referring back to Fragment VI? (Cf. 
What is Called Thinking?

 pp. 
203

 ff.) Νοεῖν, whose belonging-together with ἐόν we should like to contemplate,
 is grounded in and comes to presence from λέγειν. In
 λέγειν the letting-lie-before of what is present in its presencing occurs.
 Only as thus lying-before can what is present as such admit the
 νοεῖν, the taking-heed-of. Accordingly, the νόημα as νοούμενον of the
 νοεῖν is already a λεγόμενον of the λέγειν. In the Greek experience,
 the essence of saying rests in λέγειν. On that account νοεῖν is
 essentially—not peripherally or accidentally—something said. Certainly
 {
GA 7: 249
}
 not everything said need be an utterance. It can also, and some
 times must, be a silence.

89

Martin Heidegger (
GA 7
) Early Greek Thinking

title: Early Greek Thinking 91
headings: Martin Heidegger ( GA 7 ) Early Greek Thinking
text:
Moira (Parmenides VIII, 34-41)

 This gives us food for thought and thoroughly frees us from
 the hasty presupposition that thinking is something expressed in an
 utterance: there is nowhere any suggestion of that.

 To what extent can and must νοεῖν, thinking, come to light in the
 duality? To the extent that the unfolding in the duality of presencing
 and present beings invokes λέγειν, letting-lie-before, and with the
 released letting-lie of what lies before us, grants νοεῖν something it can
 take heed of and thus preserve. But Parmenides does not yet think the
 duality as such; he does not at all think through the unfolding of the
 twofold. He does, however, say (Frag. VIII, 35 ff.): Οὐ γὰρ ἄνευ τοῦ
 ἐόντος ... εὑρήσεις τὸ νοεῖν. "For you cannot find thinking apart
 from the duality." Why not? Because thinking belongs with ἐόν in the
 gathering that ἐόν calls for; and because thinking itself, resting in the
 λέγειν, completes the gathering called for, thus responding to its belonging
 to ἐόν as a belonging which ἐόν uses. For νοεῖν takes up, not
 just anything at random, but only that One designated in Fragment VI:
 ἐόν ἔμμεναι,* whatever is present in its presencing.

 Insofar as what is thought-provoking, though not yet thought, is
 announced in Parmenides' exposition, so far does the fundamental
 requirement clearly come to light for proper reflection upon Parmenides'
 statement that thinking belongs to Being. We have to learn to
 think the essence of language from the saying, and to think saying as
 letting-lie-before (λόγος) and as bringing-forward-into-view (φάσις).
 To satisfy this demand remains a difficult task because that first illumination
 of the essence of language as saying disappears immediately into
 a veiling darkness and yields ascendancy to a characterization of language
 which relentlessly represents it in terms of φωνή,
 vocalization—a system of signs and significations, and ultimately of
 data and information.

 *In the Ionian dialect and in epic usage the verb εἶναι (to be) may appear either as
 ἔμεναι or ἔμμεναι. In his commentary on Aristotle's 
Physics Simplicius
, for no apparent
 reason, ascribes both forms to Parmenides. The first variant appears at 144, 29 (Diels-
 Kranz VIII, 38), the second at 117, 2 (Diels-Kranz VI, 1). Heidegger reproduces the
 second variant (ἔμμεναι, DK VI, 1) throughout. With a shift of accent to the penult this
 second form becomes ἔμμεναι, an Attic isomorph—used also by Herodotus,
 however—which means to dwell in or abide by; or of things, to remain fixed, stand
 fast.—TR

91

Martin Heidegger (
GA 7
) Early Greek Thinking

GA 7: 250

title: Early Greek Thinking 92
headings: Martin Heidegger ( GA 7 ) Moira (Parmenides VIII, 34-41)
text:
EARLY GREEK THINKING

 {
GA 7: 251
}

IV

 Even now, when the way in which thinking belongs to Being has
 been brought somewhat more clearly to light, we are scarcely able to
 hear the enigmatic key word of the saying—τὸ αὐτό, the Same—in its
 enigmatic fullness. But when we see that the duality of the ἐόν, the
 presencing of what is present, gathers thinking to itself, then the governing
 duality gives us a clue to the profound riddle of what is hidden
 by the ordinarily empty and insignificant word "the Same."

 Is it from the 
unfolding
 of the twofold that the duality in turn calls
 thinking onto the path of "for its own sake," thereby requiring also the
 belonging-together of the presencing (of what is present) and thinking?
 But what is the unfolding of the twofold? How does it happen? Do we
 find any basis in Parmenides' saying for a proper inquiry into the
 unfolding of the duality, or for hearing what is essential to the unfolding
 in what the enigmatic key word of the saying silently conceals? We
 find nothing immediate.

 Still, it should occur to us that in both forms of the saying concerning
 the relation of thinking and Being the enigmatic key word stands at
 the beginning. Fragment III says, "For the Same is taking-heed-of and
 so too presencing (of what is present)." Fragment VIII, 34, says, "The
 Same is taking-heed-of and (that) toward which heedful perception is
 on the way." What does situating the word at the beginning signify in
 what this passage says? What tone is Parmenides trying to set in letting
 us hear this resounding emphasis? Ostensibly the dominant tone. In it
 resounds the anticipation of what the saying really has to say. Grammatically,
 what it says is called the predicate of the sentence. Thus the
 subject here would be νοεῖν (thinking) in its connection with εἶναι
 (Being). In accordance with the Greek text this is the sense in which
 one must interpret the grammatical structure of the saying. By placing
 its enigmatic key word at the beginning as predicate, the saying calls on
 us to dwell
 {
GA 7: 252
}
 on the word attentively, returning to it again and again. But
 even so, the word says nothing about what we would like to learn.

 Therefore we are compelled to focus our gaze relentlessly upon
 the preferred position of τὸ αὐτὸ, the Same, and to make a daring
 attempt to think from the duality of ἐόν (the presencing of what is
 present) to its unfolding.

92

Martin Heidegger (
GA 7
) Moira (Parmenides VIII, 34-41)

title: Early Greek Thinking 93
headings: Martin Heidegger ( GA 7 ) Early Greek Thinking
text:
Moira (Parmenides VIII, 34-41)

 We are aided in our purpose by the insight
 that thinking, when brought forward into view within the duality of the
 ἐόν, is something said therein, πεφατισμένον.

 As a result, what reigns in the duality is φάσις, saying as the
 invocative and insistent bringing-forward-into-view. What does the
 saying bring to appear? The presencing of what is present. The saying
 that comes to pass and governs in the duality is the gathering of presencing,
 in whose shining what is present can appear. What Parmenides
 thinks as Φύσις Heraclitus calls the Λόγος, the letting-lie-before
 that gathers.

 What happens in Φύσις and in Λόγος? Could the gathering-calling
 saying which reigns in them be that bringing which brings forth a
 shining? Which gives the lighting in whose endurance presencing is
 first illuminated, so that in its light what is present appears, thus
 governing the duality of both? Could the unfolding of the twofold
 consist in this, that a shining which illuminates itself comes to pass?
 The Greeks experience its basic character as disclosure [
Entbergen
].
 Correspondingly, disclosure reigns in the unfolding of the twofold. The
 Greeks call it Ἀλήθεια.

 If indeed Parmenides was saying something about Ἀλήθεια, he
 must have been thinking within the unfolding of the twofold. Does he
 mention Ἀλήθεια? Of course he does, right at the beginning of his
 "Didactic Poem." Even more: Ἀλήθεια is the goddess. Listening to
 what she says, Parmenides speaks his own thought—although he
 leaves unsaid what the essence of Ἀλήθεια might be rooted in. He also
 leaves unthought in what sense of divinity Ἀλήθεια is a goddess. All
 this remains for the early thinking of the Greeks as obviously outside
 the realm of the thought-provoking as any explanation of the enigmatic
 key word, τὸ αὐτὸ, the Same.
 {
GA 7: 253
}

 Presumably, however, there is some hidden link connecting all
 these unthought elements. The introductory lines of the poem (I, 22
 ff.) are not poetical finery masking an abstract conceptual work. We
 make the dialogue with Parmenides' way of thinking too easy if we
 ignore the mythic experience in the philosopher's words, and then
 object that the goddess Ἀλήθεια is an extremely vague and empty
 mental construct in comparison with the sharply delineated "divine
 persons," Hera, Athene, Demeter, Aphrodite, and Artemis.

93

Martin Heidegger (
GA 7
) Early Greek Thinking

title: Early Greek Thinking 97
headings: Martin Heidegger ( GA 7 ) Early Greek Thinking
text:
Moira (Parmenides VIII, 34-41)

 Parmenides' subordinate clause—in reality his "sentence of
 sentences"—runs (VIII, 37 ff.):

 ἐπεὶ τό γε Μοῖρ' ἐπέδησεν οὖλον ἀκίνητόν τ' ἔμμεναι:

 since Moira bound it (being) to be a whole and immovable.

 (W. Kranz)

 Parmenides speaks of ἐόν, of the presencing (of what is present), and of
 duality, and in no sense of "beings." He names the Μοῖρα, the apportionment,
 which allots by bestowing and so unfolds the twofold. The
 apportionment dispenses [
beschickt
], (provides and presents) through
 the duality. Apportionment is the dispensation of presenting, as the
 presencing of what is present, which is gathered in itself and therefore
 unfolds of itself. Μοῖρα is the destiny of "Being," in the sense of ἐόν.
 Μοῖρα has dispensed the destiny of Being, τό γε, into the duality, and
 thus has bound it to totality and immobility, from which and in which
 the presenting of what is present comes to pass.

 In the destining of duality, however, only presencing
 {
GA 7: 257
}
 attains a
 shining, and only what is present attains appearance. Destiny altogether
 conceals both the duality as such and its unfolding. The essence
 of Ἀλήθεια remains veiled. The visibility it bestows allows the
 presencing of what is present to arise as outer appearance [
Aussehen
],
 (εἶδος) and aspect [
Gesicht
], (ἰδέα). Consequently the perceptual relation
 to the presencing of what is present is defined as "seeing"
 (εἰδέναι). Stamped with this character of 
visio
, knowledge and the
 evidence of knowledge cannot renounce their essential derivation from
 luminous disclosure, even where truth has been transformed into the
 certainty of self-consciousness. 
Lumen naturale
, natural light, i.e. the
 illumination of reason, already presupposes the disclosure of the duality.
 The same holds true of the Augustinian and medieval views of
 light—not to mention their Platonic origins—which could only develop
 under the tutelage of an Ἀλήθεια already reigning in the destiny of the
 duality.

 If we wish to speak of the history of Being, we must first have
 considered that Being says: presencing of what is present: duality.

97

Martin Heidegger (
GA 7
) Early Greek Thinking

title: Early Greek Thinking 101
headings: Martin Heidegger ( GA 7 ) Early Greek Thinking
text:
Moira (Parmenides VIII, 34-41)

 {
GA 7: 261
}
 This unending dialogue is no failing. It is a sign
 of the boundlessness which, in and for remembrance, nourishes the
 possibility of a transformation of destiny.

 But anyone who only expects thinking to give assurances, and
 awaits the day when we can go beyond it as unnecessary, is demanding
 that thought annihilate itself. That demand appears in a strange light if
 we consider that the essence of mortals calls upon them to heed a call
 which beckons them toward death. As the outermost possibility of
 mortal Dasein, death is not the end of the possible but the highest
 keeping (the gathering sheltering) of the mystery of calling disclosure.

101

Martin Heidegger (
GA 7
) Early Greek Thinking

title: Early Greek Thinking 104
headings: Martin Heidegger - Lectures and Essays ( GA 7 ) Aletheia (Heraclitus, Fragment 16)
text:
EARLY GREEK THINKING

 Rather we may surmise something
 else: that we know too much and believe too readily ever to feel
 at home in a questioning which is powerfully experienced. For that we
 need the ability to wonder at what is simple, and to take up that
 wonder as our abode.
 {
GA 7: 267
}

 Of course, "simple" assertion and repetition that the literal meaning
 of άληθεσία is "unconcealment" will not give us what is simple.
 Unconcealment is the chief characteristic of that which has already
 come forward into appearance and has left concealment behind. That is
 the significance here of the α-, which only came to be classified as the
 alpha-privative by a grammar based upon later Greek thought. The
 connection with λήθη, concealment, and concealment itself do not
 diminish in importance for our thinking simply because the unconcealed
 is immediately experienced only as what has come forward in
 appearance, or what is present.

 Wonder first 
begins
 with the question, "What does all this mean
 and how could it happen?" How can we arrive at such a beginning?
 Perhaps by abandoning ourselves to a wonder which is on the lookout
 for what we call lighting and unconcealing?

 Thoughtful wonder speaks in questioning. Heraclitus says:

 τὸ μὴ δῦνόν ποτε πῶς ἄν τις λάθοι;

 How can one hide himself before that which never sets?

 (Diels-Kranz)

 The saying is numbered as Fragment 16. But because of its inner
 significance and ultimate implications, perhaps we ought to consider it
 the first. Heraclitus' saying is quoted by Clement of Alexandria in his

Paidagogos
 (Bk. III, chap. 10) to support a theological-educational position.
 He writes:

 λήσεται (!) μὲν γὰρ ἴσως τὸ αἰσθητὸν φῶς τις, τὸ δὲ νοητὸν ἀδύνατόν ἐστιν, ἢ ὥς φησιν Ἡράκλειτος ...

 "Perhaps one can hide from the light perceived by the senses, but
 it is impossible to do so before spiritual light, as Heraclitus
 says. ..." Clement is thinking about the ever-present God who sees
 everything, even the sin committed in darkness.

104

Martin Heidegger - 
Lectures and Essays
 (
GA 7
) Aletheia (Heraclitus, Fragment 16)

title: Early Greek Thinking 106
headings: Martin Heidegger - Lectures and Essays ( GA 7 ) Aletheia (Heraclitus, Fragment 16)
text:
EARLY GREEK THINKING

 The respective difference of each dialogical interpretation of
 thought is a sign of an unspoken fullness to which even Heraclitus
 himself could only speak by following the path of the insights afforded
 him. Wishing to pursue the "objectively correct" teaching of Heraclitus
 means refusing to run the salutary risk of being confounded by the
 truth of a thinking.

 The following remarks lead to no conclusions. They point toward
 the event [
das Ereignis
].

 Heraclitus' saying is a question. The word with which the fragment
 ends—"end" understood as τέλος—names that from which the
 questioning begins. It is the domain in which thinking moves. The
 word into which the question ascends is λάθοι. What could be easier to
 establish than this: that λανθάνω, aorist ἔλαθον, means "I am hidden"?
 Nonetheless, we are scarcely capable of immediately rediscovering
 just how this word speaks in Greek.

 Homer
 (
Odyssey
, VIII, 83
 ff.)
 tells how Odysseus, in the Phaeacian
 king's palace, covered his head each time at the minstrel Demodocus'
 song, whether happy or sad, and thus hidden from those present,
 wept. Verse 93 runs: ἔνθ᾽ ἄλλους μὲν πάντας ἐλάνθανε δάκρυα
 λείβων. Consistent with the spirit of our own language, we translate:
 "Then he shed tears, without all the others noticing it." The German
 translation by Voss comes closer to what the Greek says, since it carries
 the important verb ἐλάνθανε over into the German formulation: "He
 concealed his flowing tears from all the other guests." Ἐλάνθανε,
 however, does not mean the transitive "he concealed," but "he remained
 concealed" — as
 {
GA 7: 270
}
 the one who was shedding tears. "Remaining
 concealed" is the key word in the Greek. German, on the other hand,
 says: he wept, without the others noticing it. Correspondingly, we
 translate the well-known Epicurean admonition λάθε βιώσας as "Live
 in hiding." Thought from a Greek perspective, this saying means: "As
 the one who leads his life, remain concealed (therein)." Concealment
 here defines the way in which a man should be present among others.
 By the manner of its saying, the Greek announces that concealing—
 and therefore at the same time remaining unconcealed—exercises a
 commanding preeminence over every other way in which what is present
 comes to presence. The fundamental trait of presencing itself is
 determined by remaining concealed and unconcealed.

106

Martin Heidegger - 
Lectures and Essays
 (
GA 7
) Aletheia (Heraclitus, Fragment 16)

title: Early Greek Thinking 109
headings: Martin Heidegger ( GA 7 ) Early Greek Thinking
text:
Aletheia (Heraclitus, Fragment B 16)

 Thus they also identify the concealment
 into which man falls by reference to its relation to what is withdrawn
 from him by concealment.

 Both in the way the Greek employs λανθάνειν, to remain concealed,
 as a basic and predominant verb, as well as in the experience of
 the forgetting of remaining-concealed, this much is made sufficiently
 clear: λανθάνω, I remain concealed, does not signify just a form of
 human behavior among many others, but identifies the basic trait
 {
GA 7: 273
}
 of
 every response to what is present or absent—if not, indeed, the basic
 trait of presence and absence themselves.

 Now, if this word λήθω, I remain concealed, speaks to us in the
 saying of a thinker, and if perhaps it concludes a thoughtful question,
 then we are bound to ponder the word and what it says as comprehensively
 and as persistently as we can today.

 Every remaining-concealed includes a relation to the sort of thing
 from which the concealed has withdrawn, but toward which in many
 cases it remains directly inclined. The Greek names in the accusative
 that to which what has withdrawn into concealment remains related:
 ἐνθ' ἄλλους μὲν πάντας ἐλάνθανε.

 Heraclitus asks: πῶς ἄν τις λάθοι "how could anyone remain
 concealed?" Relative to what? To what is named in the preceding
 words, with which the fragment begins: τὸ μὴ δῦνόν ποτε, that which
 never sets. The "anyone" mentioned here is consequently not the
 subject in relation to which something else remains concealed, but the
 "anyone" who comes into question with respect to the possibility of his
 own remaining-concealed. Heraclitus' question is not first and
 foremost a consideration of concealment and unconcealment with regard
 to the sort of men whom we, with our modern habits of representation,
 like to interpret as carriers—or even creators—of unconcealment.
 Heraclitus' question, expressed in modern terms, thinks the
 reverse. It ponders the relation of man to "the never-setting" and
 thinks human being from this relation.

 With the words "the never-setting" we are translating—as though
 it were self-evident—the Greek phrase τὸ μὴ δῦνόν ποτε. What do
 these words signify? Where do we get our information about them?
 This seems the obvious question to explore, even if the pursuit should
 lead us far from the saying of Heraclitus.

109

Martin Heidegger (
GA 7
) Early Greek Thinking

title: Early Greek Thinking 118
headings: Martin Heidegger - Lectures and Essays ( GA 7 ) Aletheia (Heraclitus, Fragment 16)
text:
EARLY GREEK THINKING

 The meditative fire is the gathering which lays everything
 there before us (into presenting). Τὸ Πῦρ is ὁ Λόγος. Its meditating is
 the heart, i.e. the lighting-sheltering expanse, of the world. In a multiplicity
 of different names—φύσις, πῦρ, λόγος, ἁρμονίη, πόλεμος, ἕρις,
 (φιλία), ἕν— Heraclitus thinks the essential fullness of the Same.

 From beginning to end and back again this list refers to the phrase
 that begins 
Fragment 16
:
 τὸ μὴ δῦνόν ποτε, the not setting ever. What
 is named in it must be heard in consonance with all those fundamental
 words of Heraclitean thinking to which we have referred.

 In the meantime, we have seen that never entering into concealment
 is the enduring rising out of self-concealing. In this way does the
 world fire glow and shine and meditate. If we think it as lighting, this
 includes not only the brilliance, but also the openness wherein everything,
 especially the reciprocally related, comes into shining. Lighting
 is therefore more than illuminating, and also more than laying bare.
 Lighting is the meditatively gathering bringing-before into the open. It
 is the bestowal of presenting.

 The event of lighting is the world. The meditatively gathering
 lighting which brings into the open is revealing; it abides in self-concealing.
 Self-concealing belongs to it as that which finds its essence
 in revealing, and which therefore cannot ever be a mere going into
 concealment, never a setting.

 Πως ἄν τις λάθοι; "How then could anyone remain concealed?"
 the fragment asks, with reference to the forementioned τὸ μὴ δῦνόν
 ποτε, which stands in the accusative. In translating, we make it the
 object of a preposition in the dative case—"How could anyone remain
 hidden before it, that is, before the lighting?" Without giving a reason,
 the form of the question rejects such a possibility. The reason must
 already lie in what is questioned itself. All too quickly we are prepared
 to bring it forward: since the never-setting, the lighting,
 {
GA 7: 284
}
 sees and
 notices everything, nothing can hide before it. But there is no mention
 of seeing and noticing in the fragment. Above all, however, the fragment
 does not say πῶς ἄν τι, "how could something ...?" but πῶς ἄν
 τις, "how could someone ...?" According to the fragment, the lighting
 is in no way related to whatever just happens to be present. Who is
 meant by the τίς?

118

title: Early Greek Thinking 120
headings: Martin Heidegger - Lectures and Essays ( GA 7 ) Aletheia (Heraclitus, Fragment 16)
text:
EARLY GREEK THINKING

 Why is it that they cannot? Because
 their relation to the lighting is nothing other than the lighting
 itself, in that this relation gathers men and gods into the lighting and
 keeps them there.

 The lighting not only illuminates what is present, but gathers it
 together and secures it in advance in presencing. But of what sort is the
 presenting of gods and men? They are not only illuminated in the
 lighting, but are also enlightened from it and toward it. Thus they can,
 in 
their
 way, accomplish the lighting (bring it to the fullness of its
 essence) and thereby protect it. Gods and men are not only lighted by a
 light—even if a supersensible one—so that they can never hide themselves
 from it in darkness; they are luminous in their essence. They are
 alight [
er-lichtet
]; they are appropriated into the event of lighting, and
 therefore never concealed. On the contrary, they are re-vealed,
 thought in still another sense. Just as those who are far distant belong
 to the distance, so are the revealed—in the sense now to be thought
 —entrusted to the lighting that keeps and shelters them. According to
 their essence, they are trans-posed [
ver-legt
] to the concealing of the
 mystery, gathered together, belonging to the Λόγος in ὁμολογεΐν
 (
Fragment 50
).

 Did Heraclitus intend his question as we have just been discussing
 it? Was what this discussion has said within the range of his notions?
 {
GA 7: 286
}
 Who knows? Who can say? But perhaps the fragment, independendy
 of Heraclitus' own representational range, says the sort of thing our
 tentative discussion has put forward. The fragment does say it—
 provided a thoughtful dialogue may bring it to speak. The fragment
 says it, and leaves it unuttered. The paths that lead through the region
 of the unuttered remain questions, questions which always evoke only
 such things as were manifested long ago on those paths under diverse
 disguises.

 The fundamentally interrogative character of the fragment indicates
 that Heraclitus is contemplating the revealing-concealing lighting,
 the world fire, in its scarcely perceptible relation to those who are
 en-lightened in accord with their essence, and who therefore hearken
 to and belong to the lighting in an exceptional way.

 Or does the fragment speak out of an experience of thinking which
 has already weighed every step? Might Heraclitus' question only be
 saying that evidently there is no way possible for the relation of the
 world fire to gods and men to be other than this: gods and men belong
 in the lighting not only as lighted and viewed, but also as invisible,
 bringing the lighting with them in their own way, preserving it and
 handing it down in its endurance?

120

title: Early Greek Thinking 121
headings: Martin Heidegger ( GA 7 ) Early Greek Thinking
text:
Aletheia (Heraclitus, Fragment B 16)

 In this case the fragment, with its questioning, could give voice to
 a thoughtful wonder, which stands expectantly [
verhofft
] before that
 relation wherein the lighting takes the essence of gods and men unto
 itself. The questioning saying would then correspond to what is ever
 and again worthy of wonder and is preserved in its worth by wonder.

 It is impossible to estimate how much and how clearly Heraclitus'
 thinking presaged the realm of all realms. That the fragment moves
 within the realm of the lighting cannot be doubted as soon as we
 consider ever more clearly this one matter: the beginning and the end
 of the fragment name revealing and concealing—particularly with respect
 to their interconnection. We do not even require a separate reference
 to Fragment 50, in which the revealing-concealing gathering is
 identified as being entrusted to
 {
GA 7: 287
}
 mortals in such a way that their essence
 unfolds in this: their correspondence or noncorrespondence to the
 Λόγος.

 We are too quick to believe that the mystery of what is to be
 thought always lies distant and deeply hidden under a hardly penetrable
 layer of strangeness. On the contrary, it has its essential abode in
 what is near by, which approaches what is coming into presence and
 preserves what has drawn near. The presenting of the near is too close
 for our customary mode of representational thought—which exhausts
 itself in securing what is present—to experience the governance of the
 near, and without preparation to think it adequately. Presumably, the
 mystery that beckons in what is to be thought is nothing other than
 essentially what we have attempted to suggest in the name the "lighting."
 Everyday opinion, therefore, self-assuredly and stubbornly
 bypasses the mystery. Heraclitus knew this. Fragment 72 runs:

 ὧι μάλιστα διηνεκῶς ὁμιλοῦσι Λόγωι τούτωι διὰφέρονται,
 καὶ οἷς καθ΄ ἡμέραν ἐγκυροῦσι, ταῦτα αὐτοῖς ξένα φαίνεται.

 From that to which for the most part they are bound and by which they are
 thoroughly sustained, the Λόγος, from that they separate themselves; and it
 becomes manifest: whatever they daily encounter remains foreign (in its presenting)
 to them.*

 * Diels-Kranz (I, 167) translate, "... from the Meaning with which for the most
 part they go about (from that which governs the totality), from that they separate themselves,
 and the things they encounter every day seem strange to them." A more fluent
 translation appears in the excellent French collection by Jean Brun,

Héraclite, ou le philosophe de l'eternel retour

 (Paris: Seghers, 1965), p. 188: "However closely united
 they are to the Logos which governs the world, they separate themselves from it,
 etc."—TH.

121

Martin Heidegger (
GA 7
) Early Greek Thinking

title: Early Greek Thinking 122
headings: Martin Heidegger - Lectures and Essays ( GA 7 ) Aletheia (Heraclitus, Fragment 16)
text:
EARLY GREEK THINKING

 Mortals are irrevocably bound to the revealing-concealing gathering
 which lights everything present in its presencing. But they turn
 from the lighting, and turn only toward what is present, which is what
 immediately concerns them in their everyday commerce with each
 other. They believe that this trafficking in what is present by itself
 creates for them a sufficient familiarity with it. But it nonetheless
 remains foreign to them. For they have no inkling of what they have
 been entrusted with: presencing, which in its lighting first allows what
 is present to come to appearance. Λόγος, in whose lighting they come
 and go, remains concealed from them, and forgotten.

 {
GA 7: 288
}
 The more familiar to them everything knowable becomes, the
 more foreign it is to them—without their being able to know this. They
 would become aware of all this if only they would ask: how could
 anyone whose essence belongs to the lighting ever withdraw from
 receiving and protecting the lighting? How could he, without immediately
 discovering that the everyday can seem quite ordinary to
 him only because this ordinariness is guilty of forgetting what initially
 brings even the apparently self-evident into the light of what is present?

 Everyday opinion seeks truth in variety, the endless variety of
 novelties which are displayed before it. It does not see the quiet gleam
 (the gold) of the mystery that everlastingly shines in the simplicity of
 the lighting. Heraclitus says
 (
Fragment 9
):

 ὄνους σύρματ' ἂν ἑλέσθαι μᾶλλον ἢ χρυσόν.

 "Asses choose hay rather than gold."

122

Martin Heidegger - 
Lectures and Essays
 (
GA 7
) Aletheia (Heraclitus, Fragment 16)

title: Early Greek Thinking 123
headings: Martin Heidegger ( GA 7 ) Early Greek Thinking
text:
Aletheia (Heraclitus, Fragment B 16)

 But the golden gleam of the lighting's invisible shining cannot be
 grasped, because it is not itself something grasping. Rather, it is the
 purely appropriating event [
das reine Ereignen
]. The invisible shining
 of the lighting streams from wholesome self-keeping in the self-restraining
 preservation of destiny. Therefore the shining of the lighting
 is in itself at the same time a self-veiling—and is in that sense what
 is most obscure.

 Heraclitus is called ὁ Σκοτεινός. He will also retain this name in
 the future. He is the Obscure, because he thinks questioningly into the
 lighting.

1
ἀλήθεια (alētheia)
veritas
Wahrheit
truth / unconcealment
ἀλήθεια originally means 
un‑hiddenness
, the state in which beings emerge from concealment. Heidegger insists that the Latin 
veritas
 distorts this by reducing truth to correctness. For the early Greeks, ἀλήθεια names the event in which beings show themselves. It is not a property of propositions but a happening of Being. Heidegger reactivates this primordial sense to critique the history of metaphysics.

2
λόγος (logos)
ratio
Logos / Rede
gathering / saying
For the Presocratics, λόγος means the gathering that lets something appear as what it is. It is not primarily “speech” or “reason” but the structural articulation of Being. Heraclitus uses λόγος to name the underlying order of the cosmos. Heidegger interprets λόγος as 
legein
, the gathering that lets beings lie before us. The Latin 
ratio
 narrows it into calculative reason.

3
φύσις (physis)
natura
Natur
emerging‑abiding sway
φύσις originally means the self‑emergence of beings into presence. It is not “nature” as a domain of objects but the dynamic unfolding of Being. Heidegger emphasizes that φύσις is the earliest Greek name for Being itself. It names the rising‑up and abiding of beings. Latin 
natura
 freezes this dynamic into a static category.

4
ὄν / τὰ ὄντα (on / ta onta)
ens / entia
Seiendes
beings
ὄν is the participle “being,” and τὰ ὄντα means “the beings” in their totality. Heidegger stresses that the Greeks did not yet distinguish “being” from “beings” in the later metaphysical sense. For Anaximander, τὰ ὄντα includes natural, human, divine, and artificial beings. Heidegger uses 
Seiendes
 to mark the ontic realm. The question of Being arises only when beings are seen as beings.

5
εἶναι (einai)
esse
Sein
to be / Being
εἶναι is the infinitive “to be,” but for the Greeks it names the event of presence. Heidegger argues that the Greeks experienced Being as 
presence
 (Anwesen). Latin 
esse
 transforms Being into a static property. Heidegger’s 
Sein
 attempts to retrieve the dynamic, temporal character of εἶναι. The forgetting of Being begins when εἶναι becomes a universal concept.

6
γένεσις (genesis)
generatio
Entstehen 
emergence / presencing
γένεσις means the coming‑forth of beings into presence. It is not merely biological birth or physical origin. Heidegger interprets γένεσις as the event of presencing (Anwesen). In Anaximander, γένεσις is paired with φθορά as two modes of Being’s temporal unfolding. Latin 
generatio
 narrows it to biological or causal production.

7
φθορά (phthora)
corruptio
Vergehen
withdrawal / departure
φθορά is usually translated as “decay,” but Heidegger hears it as the counter‑movement to γένεσις. It names the departure of beings from presence, their withdrawal into absence. This is not destruction but a necessary mode of Being’s temporal play. Latin 
corruptio
 moralizes and materializes the term. Heidegger links φθορά to 
Abwesen
 (absence).

8
χρεών (chreōn)
debitum / necessitas
das Notwendige
the must of Being
χρεών is often rendered “necessity,” but Heidegger interprets it as the inner “must” of Being’s unfolding. It is not a law imposed from outside but the essential requirement of presencing and absencing. In Anaximander, beings emerge and withdraw “according to the χρεών.” This expresses the inner lawfulness of Being itself. Latin 
necessitas
 distorts it into compulsion.

9
δίκη (dikē)
iustitia
Fuge / Fug
fittingness / jointure
δίκη is not moral justice but the fitting order of Being. Heidegger interprets δίκη as the 
jointure
 (Fug) that lets beings appear in their proper measure. It is the structural balance of presencing and absencing. In Anaximander, δίκη names the ontological order that governs beings. Latin 
iustitia
 moralizes the term.

10
ἀδικία (adikia)
iniustitia
Un‑Fug
dis‑measure / overstepping
ἀδικία is not moral wrongdoing but ontological overstepping. It names the tendency of beings to persist, dominate, or exceed their allotted measure. Heidegger interprets ἀδικία as the disturbance of δίκη. It is the imbalance inherent in beings’ striving to presence. Latin 
iniustitia
 reduces it to ethical fault.

11
τίσις (tisis)
poena / retributio
Ausgleich
re‑balancing / giving‑back
τίσις is usually translated as “penalty,” but Heidegger hears it as the restoring of balance. It is the counter‑movement that returns beings to their proper measure. In Anaximander, beings “give back” to one another for their overstepping. This is not punishment but ontological compensation. Latin poena moralizes it.

12
χρόνος (chronos)
tempus
Zeit
time as presencing
χρόνος is not clock‑time but the temporal stretching in which beings appear and withdraw. Heidegger interprets χρόνος as the ecstatic structure of presencing. It is the horizon that allows γένεσις and φθορά to occur. Latin tempus abstracts it into a measurable sequence. Heidegger’s Zeit retrieves its ontological depth.

13
τάξις (taxis)
ordo
Ordnung
ordering / articulation
τάξις means the ordering or arrangement that structures presencing. In Anaximander, “the τάξις of time” is the articulation of temporal unfolding. Heidegger interprets τάξις as the structural jointure of Being. It is not a law but an ordering. Latin ordo narrows it to hierarchical arrangement.

14
ἄπειρον (apeiron)
infinitum
das Unbegrenzte
the boundless
For Anaximander, ἄπειρον is the boundless source from which beings emerge. It is not infinite in the mathematical sense but without determinate limits. Heidegger interprets it as the primordial openness of Being. It is the origin that is not itself a being. Latin infinitum misleads by suggesting endless extension.

15
ἔρις (eris)
discordia
Streit
strife
Heraclitus uses ἔρις to name the productive tension that holds the cosmos together. It is not mere conflict but the dynamic interplay of opposites. Heidegger interprets ἔρις as the strife that constitutes world. It is the ontological tension that allows beings to appear. Latin discordia moralizes it.

16
πόλεμος (polemos)
bellum
Kampf
war / conflict as origin
Heraclitus calls πόλεμος “the father of all.” Heidegger interprets this not as literal war but as the primordial conflict that differentiates beings. It is the strife that sets limits and opens world. Polemos is the ontological event of differentiation. Latin bellum reduces it to military conflict.

17
μοῖρα (moira)
fatum
Geschick
destiny / allotment
μοῖρα means the portion or share allotted to each being. Heidegger links it to Geschick, the sending of Being. It is not fatalistic determinism but the structural distribution of presencing. In early Greek thought, μοῖρα governs measure. Latin fatum distorts it into predestination.

18
ἦθος (ēthos)
mos
Sitte
dwelling / character
ἦθος originally means dwelling place, the habitual abode. Heidegger retrieves this sense to interpret Heraclitus’ fragment “ἦθος ἀνθρώπῳ δαίμων.” Ethos is the place where human beings dwell in relation to Being. It is not moral character but existential dwelling. Latin mos moralizes it.

19
δαίμων (daimōn)
daemon
das Dämonische
the guiding spirit
δαίμων is not a demon but a divine‑human intermediary. For Heraclitus, it names the guiding force of one’s destiny. Heidegger interprets δαίμων as the way Being addresses a human being. It is the voice of destiny. Latin daemon later becomes associated with evil.

20
λόγος ὁμολογεῖν (logos homologein)
confessio
Zuspruch
attunement to the logos
ὁμολογεῖν means “to say the same as,” to be attuned to the λόγος. Heidegger interprets this as listening to the gathering of Being. It is not agreement but existential attunement. Heraclitus says most fail to ὁμολογεῖν. Latin confessio misses the ontological sense.

21
παρὼν / ἀπών (parōn / apōn)
praesens / absens
anwesend / abwesend
present / absent
These terms name modes of presencing. Heidegger uses them to show that Being is temporal. Presence is not static but an event. Absence is not non‑being but another mode of Being’s play. Latin praesens and absens flatten the dynamic.

22
ἔστι (esti)
est
ist
is
The simple verb “is” becomes the central question of Western metaphysics. Heidegger shows how Parmenides’ “ἐστίν” grounds the history of Being. The Greeks experienced “is” as presence. Latin est becomes a copula. Heidegger reopens the question of the “is.”

23
νοεῖν (noein)
intelligere
Vernehmen
to apprehend / to heed
For Parmenides, νοεῖν is the apprehension of Being. Heidegger interprets it as Vernehmen, a receptive heeding. It is not conceptual thinking but letting‑be. Latin intelligere intellectualizes it. Noein is the mode of access to Being.

24
λέγειν (legein)
dicere
sagen
to gather / to say
λέγειν originally means to gather, to lay out. Heidegger emphasizes this as the root of λόγος. Saying is gathering. Latin dicere reduces it to speaking. Heidegger retrieves the gathering sense.

25
ὁδός (hodos)
via
Weg
way / path
ὁδός means way or path. Parmenides’ poem is structured as a journey along the way of Being. Heidegger interprets ὁδός as the path of thinking. It is not a metaphor but the structure of access to Being. Latin via keeps some of this sense but loses the ontological depth.

26
ἄλη (alē)
verum
das Wahre
the true / the unconcealed
ἄλη is an older form related to ἀλήθεια, emphasizing the state of being unhidden. It names the primordial openness in which beings can appear. Heidegger sees in this root the earliest Greek experience of truth as unconcealment. It predates the propositional sense of truth. Latin verum shifts the meaning toward correctness.

27
ἔν (hen)
unum
Eins
the One
For Parmenides, ἔν names the unity of Being. It is not numerical oneness but the indivisible wholeness of presence. Heidegger interprets the One as the unifying event of Being. It is not a highest being but the unity of presencing. Latin unum misleads by suggesting a countable entity.

28
ἔστι γάρ εἶναι (esti gar einai)
est enim esse
denn Sein ist
for Being is
This Parmenidean phrase grounds Western ontology. It asserts that Being is, and non‑being is not. Heidegger interprets it as the primordial insight into the self‑showing of Being. It is not a logical axiom but an experiential disclosure. Latin est enim esse reduces it to a tautology.

29
μῦθος (mythos)
fabula
Sage
myth / saying
μῦθος originally means a significant saying or utterance. It is not opposed to λόγος in early Greek thought. Heidegger emphasizes that μῦθος is a mode of revealing. Only later does it become “myth” in the sense of fiction. Latin fabula contributes to this decline.

30
φύλαξ (phylax)
custos
Wächter
guardian
In Parmenides’ proem, the goddess is a guardian of the way of truth. Heidegger interprets φύλαξ as the one who keeps open the clearing of Being. It is not a mere protector but a preserver of unconcealment. Latin custos narrows it to a watchman. The term resonates with Heidegger’s idea of “the shepherd of Being.”

31
ἄνθρωπος (anthrōpos)
homo
Mensch
human being
ἄνθρωπος originally means the one who “looks up” or “faces upward.” Heidegger interprets the human as the being who stands in the clearing of Being. The human is not defined by rationality but by openness to Being. Latin homo shifts the focus to biological species. Heidegger’s Mensch is existential, not zoological.

32
ψυχή (psychē)
anima
Seele
soul / animating principle
ψυχή originally means breath or life‑force. For early Greeks, it is the principle of animation, not an immortal substance. Heidegger interprets ψυχή as a mode of Being‑in‑the‑world. Latin anima spiritualizes it. Later metaphysics turns ψυχή into a metaphysical entity.

33
νοῦς (nous)
intellectus
Geist
mind / intuitive apprehension
νοῦς is the faculty of direct apprehension of Being. It is not discursive reasoning but immediate insight. Heidegger sees νοῦς as a primordial mode of openness. Latin intellectus intellectualizes it. In Anaxagoras, νοῦς becomes a cosmic ordering principle.

34
ἔθος (ethos)
consuetudo
Gewohnheit
habit / custom
ἔθος is related to ἦθος but emphasizes habitual dwelling. Heidegger uses it to show how human existence is shaped by habitual ways of being. It is not merely social custom but existential patterning. Latin consuetudo narrows it to social habit.

35
ἄξιος (axios)
dignus
würdig
worthy / fitting
ἄξιος means worthy or fitting. Heidegger interprets it in relation to δίκη: beings are worthy insofar as they fit into the order of presencing. Worth is ontological, not moral. Latin dignus moralizes it. The term anticipates Heidegger’s notion of Würdigkeit (worthiness for Being).

36
ἔριον (erion)
lana
Wolle
wool / thread (metaphorical)
Used metaphorically in early Greek thought to describe the weaving of fate or order. Heidegger sometimes invokes weaving metaphors to describe the interlacing of presencing and absencing. The term suggests the texture of Being. Latin lana loses the metaphorical richness.

37
ἄναξ (anax)
dominus
Herr
lord / master
ἄναξ is a title for gods and kings. Heidegger uses it to illuminate the early Greek sense of divine ordering. It is not domination but presiding over the clearing. Latin dominus shifts toward ownership. Heidegger’s Herr is existential, not feudal.

38
δαίς (dais)
convivium
Mahl
feast / distribution
In Homeric Greek, δαίς refers to a feast where portions are distributed. Heidegger uses it metaphorically to describe the distribution of Being. It resonates with μοῖρα (allotment). Latin convivium misses the distributive nuance.

39
ἄγαλμα (agalma)
simulacrum
Abbild
image / shining‑forth
ἄγαλμα means a statue or image that shines with divine presence. Heidegger interprets it as a site where Being appears. It is not representation but manifestation. Latin simulacrum reduces it to imitation. The term anticipates Heidegger’s analysis of the artwork.

40
ἔργον (ergon)
opus
Werk
work / deed
ἔργον means work, deed, or accomplishment. Heidegger interprets it as the bringing‑forth of beings into presence. It is not mere labor but ontological production. Latin opus narrows it to product. Heidegger’s Werk is a site of world‑opening.

41
τέχνη (technē)
ars
Kunst / Technik
craft / bringing‑forth
τέχνη originally means a mode of revealing. It is not technology in the modern sense. Heidegger interprets τέχνη as a way in which truth happens. It is a bringing‑forth (Hervorbringen). Latin ars shifts toward skill. Modern Technik distorts it into instrumental control.

42
ποίησις (poiēsis)
poesis
Dichtung
bringing‑forth / poetry
ποίησις is the act of bringing something into presence. It is not limited to literary poetry. Heidegger interprets it as a fundamental mode of revealing. All creation is a kind of ποίησις. Latin poesis narrows it to literature.

43
ἀρχή (archē)
principium
Anfang / Ursprung
origin / principle
ἀρχή means beginning, origin, or ruling principle. For the Presocratics, it names the fundamental source of beings. Heidegger interprets ἀρχή as the primordial ground of presencing. It is not a cause but an originating sway. Latin principium shifts toward logical principle.

44
τέλος (telos)
finis
Ziel / Zweck
end / fulfillment
τέλος means completion or fulfillment, not termination. Heidegger interprets it as the consummation of presencing. It is the point at which something fully appears as what it is. Latin finis confuses it with cessation. Heidegger’s Ziel preserves the sense of fulfillment.

45
μέτρον (metron)
mensura
Maß
measure
μέτρον is central to Greek thought: everything has its measure. Heidegger interprets measure as the fittingness of beings within the clearing. It is not quantitative but ontological. Latin mensura narrows it to measurement. Heidegger’s Maß is existential.

46
ὕβρις (hybris)
superbia
Übermaß
excess / overreaching
ὕβρις is overstepping one’s measure. Heidegger links it to ἀδικία. It is not moral arrogance but ontological excess. Beings tend to assert themselves beyond their allotted place. Latin superbia moralizes it.

47
ἁρμονία (harmonia)
concordia
Fügung
harmony / fitting‑together
ἁρμονία means the fitting‑together of opposites. Heraclitus uses it to describe the hidden unity of strife. Heidegger interprets it as the jointure of Being. It is not aesthetic harmony but ontological articulation. Latin concordia moralizes it.

48
πῦρ (pyr)
ignis
Feuer
fire
For Heraclitus, fire is the metaphor for the ever‑living flux of Being. It symbolizes transformation and measure. Heidegger interprets fire as the dynamic presencing of Being. It is not a physical element but an ontological symbol. Latin ignis loses the metaphysical depth.

49
κόσμος (kosmos)
mundus
Welt
world / order
κόσμος originally means order, arrangement, adornment. It is not the universe as a container but the ordered whole of beings. Heidegger interprets κόσμος as world, the open region where beings appear. Latin mundus shifts toward a physical universe. Heidegger’s Welt is existential.

50
φύλαξις (phylaxis)
tutela
Bewahrung
preservation
φύλαξις means guarding or preserving. Heidegger uses it to describe the task of thinking: to preserve the truth of Being. It is not protection from danger but safeguarding unconcealment. Latin tutela narrows it to legal guardianship. Heidegger’s Bewahrung is ontological.

51
ἀνάγκη (anankē)
necessitas
Not / Zwang
necessity / compulsion
ἀνάγκη in early Greek thought names a binding force that even gods cannot escape. It is not logical necessity but the compelling sway of Being. Heidegger distinguishes ἀνάγκη from χρεών: the former is constraining, the latter is the inner “must” of presencing. In tragedy, ἀνάγκη marks the inescapable structure of fate. Latin necessitas flattens it into logical or causal necessity.

52
ἔθος / ἦθος (ethos)
mos / consuetudo
Sitte / Brauch
dwelling / habitual comportment
Though often translated as “ethics,” ἦθος originally means dwelling place or habitual abode. Heidegger retrieves this meaning to interpret Heraclitus’ fragment “ἦθος ἀνθρώπῳ δαίμων.” Ethos is the place where human beings dwell in relation to Being. It is not moral character but existential attunement. Latin mos moralizes it.

53
ἄγος (agos)
sacrum
das Heilige
the sacred / taboo
ἄγος refers to something sacred or taboo, often associated with divine prohibition. Heidegger interprets it as the dimension of the holy that precedes the gods. It marks the uncanny region where Being withdraws. It is not moral impurity but ontological danger. Latin sacrum narrows it to religious holiness.

54
ἄγχι (agchi)
prope
Nähe
nearness
ἄγχι means “near” or “close.” Heidegger uses nearness to describe the way Being approaches without becoming present. Nearness is not spatial proximity but existential intimacy. The gods are near even when absent. Latin prope lacks this ontological nuance.

55
ἀλήθευμα (alētheuma)
veritas
Wahrheitsgeschehen
truth‑event
ἀλήθευμα is a derivative of ἀλήθεια, meaning a truth or disclosure. Heidegger interprets it as an event in which beings emerge from concealment. It is not a proposition but a happening. Truth is something that occurs, not something possessed. Latin veritas reduces it to correctness.

56
ἄρρητον (arrhēton)
ineffabile
das Unsagbare
the unsayable
ἄρρητον means that which cannot be spoken. For the Greeks, this is not because of mystical ineffability but because Being exceeds conceptual grasp. Heidegger interprets the unsayable as the withdrawal of Being. It is not irrational but pre‑conceptual. Latin ineffabile spiritualizes it.

57
ἄρχειν (archein)
principari
herrschen
to rule / to begin
ἄρχειν means both to rule and to begin. Heidegger emphasizes this dual meaning to show that the origin (ἀρχή) is also the ruling principle. Being rules by beginning. Latin principari loses the ontological depth. Heidegger’s herrschen is existential, not political.

58
ἀρχή (archē)
principium
Ursprung
origin / source
Although we covered ἀρχή earlier, here we emphasize its role in Heidegger’s reading of the Presocratics. ἀρχή is not a first cause but the originating sway. It is the source that gives rise without itself being a being. Heidegger interprets it as the primordial ground of presencing. Latin principium reduces it to logical principle.

59
ἄρτιος (artios)
perfectus
vollkommen
complete / fitting
ἄρτιος means complete, perfect, or fitting. Heidegger uses it to describe the completeness of presencing when beings appear fully as themselves. It is not moral perfection but ontological fulfillment. Latin perfectus shifts toward moral or aesthetic perfection.

60
ἀσφάλεια (asphaleia)
securitas
Sicherheit
security / stability
ἀσφάλεια originally means firmness or stability. Heidegger interprets it as the stability of the clearing that allows beings to appear. It is not psychological security but ontological steadiness. Latin securitas becomes subjective. Heidegger’s Sicherheit is structural.

61
ἀταραξία (ataraxia)
tranquillitas
Gelassenheit
tranquility / letting‑be
ἀταραξία means unperturbedness. Heidegger links it to Gelassenheit, the letting‑be of beings. It is not emotional calm but existential openness. The term anticipates Heidegger’s later thought on releasement. Latin tranquillitas psychologizes it.

62
ἀτιμία (atimia)
ignominia
Ehrlosigkeit
dishonor / lack of worth
ἀτιμία means lack of honor or worth. Heidegger interprets it ontologically as the failure to dwell in the clearing of Being. It is not social shame but existential impoverishment. Latin ignominia moralizes it. The term contrasts with ἄξιος (worthy).

63
αὐγή (augē)
radius
Glanz
radiance / gleam
αὐγή means radiance or gleam. Heidegger uses it to describe the shining‑forth of beings in unconcealment. It is not physical light but ontological luminosity. Latin radius reduces it to a ray. Heidegger’s Glanz preserves the metaphysical sense.

64
βίος (bios)
vita
Leben
life
βίος means life in the sense of a way of living. Heidegger distinguishes it from ζωή (life as biological vitality). Bios is existential life. It is the manner in which a human being dwells. Latin vita conflates both senses.

65
γνῶσις (gnōsis)
cognitio
Erkenntnis
knowing / insight
γνῶσις is knowledge as insight, not as information. Heidegger interprets it as a mode of disclosure. It is not representational but participatory. Latin cognitio intellectualizes it. Heidegger’s Erkenntnis is always grounded in Being.

66
δαίμων (daimōn)
daemon
Dämon
guiding spirit
Although covered earlier, here we emphasize its role in Heidegger’s reading of Heraclitus. The daimōn is the guiding force of one’s destiny. It is not a supernatural being but the way Being addresses a human. Latin daemon later becomes demonic.

67
δέος (deos)
timor
Furcht
fear / awe
δέος means fear or awe. Heidegger interprets it as the existential mood that opens the human to Being. It is not psychological fear but ontological trembling. Latin timor narrows it. Heidegger’s Furcht is a basic mood.

68
δέσποινα (despoina)
domina
Herrin
mistress / lady
In Parmenides’ proem, the goddess is addressed as δέσποινα. Heidegger interprets her as the presencing of truth itself. She is not a mythological figure but the personification of ἀλήθεια. Latin domina loses the ontological dimension.

69
διάνοια (dianoia)
discursus
Denken / Verstand
discursive thinking
διάνοια is discursive, step‑by‑step thinking. Heidegger contrasts it with νοῦς (intuitive apprehension). It is necessary but secondary. Latin discursus captures the movement but not the ontological grounding. Heidegger’s Verstand is calculative.

70
δίκη (dikē)
iustitia
Fug
fittingness / justice
Reiterated here to emphasize its centrality. δίκη is the structural order of Being. It is not moral justice but ontological jointure. Heidegger’s Fug captures this sense. Latin iustitia moralizes it.

71
δόξα (doxa)
opinio
Meinung
opinion / seeming
δόξα means appearance or seeming. For Parmenides, it is the realm of mortal opinion. Heidegger interprets δόξα as the everyday understanding of Being. It is not false but superficial. Latin opinio reduces it to subjective belief.

72
δύναμις (dynamis)
potentia
Möglichkeit
power / potentiality
δύναμις means potentiality or capacity. Heidegger interprets it as the possibility inherent in Being. It is not mere ability but ontological potential. Latin potentia shifts toward force. Heidegger’s Möglichkeit is existential.

73
εἶδος (eidos)
forma
Form
form / look
εἶδος originally means the look or appearance of something. Plato later turns it into the Idea. Heidegger retrieves the earlier sense: the way a being shows itself. Latin forma narrows it. Heidegger’s Form is phenomenological.

74
ἔθος (ethos)
habitus
Gewohnheit
habit / custom
Reiterated here to emphasize its existential meaning. Ethos is the habitual dwelling of human beings. It shapes how beings appear. Latin habitus shifts toward moral character.

75
ζῆν (zēn)
vivere
leben
to live
ζῆν means to live in the biological sense. Heidegger distinguishes it from existieren, which is uniquely human. Animals live; humans exist. Latin vivere conflates both. ζῆν is the basis for higher modes of Being.

76
ζῷον (zōion)
animal
Lebewesen
living being
ζῷον means a living creature, but not in the modern biological sense. For the Greeks, a ζῷον is defined by its capacity for perception and movement. Heidegger uses the term to distinguish animal life from human existence: animals are “poor in world,” whereas humans are “world‑forming.” Latin animal narrows the meaning to biological classification. Heidegger’s Lebewesen preserves the existential nuance.

77
ζωή (zōē)
vita
Leben
life (as vitality)
ζωή refers to life as sheer vitality, the fact of being alive. It contrasts with βίος, which means a way of life. Heidegger uses ζωή to mark the biological dimension of beings. It is the basis for higher modes of Being but not equivalent to human existence. Latin vita conflates ζωή and βίος.

78
ἔντεχνος (entechnos)
artifex
kunstvoll
skillful / artful
ἔντεχνος means “within the domain of τέχνη,” i.e., skillfully crafted. Heidegger uses it to show how early Greek thought saw craft as a mode of revealing. It is not mere technical proficiency but a way of bringing‑forth. Latin artifex reduces it to craftsmanship. Heidegger’s kunstvoll retains the ontological sense.

79
ἔνθεος (entheos)
inspiratus
begeistert
inspired / possessed by the divine
ἔνθεος literally means “in‑god,” indicating divine inspiration. Heidegger interprets it as a mode of ecstatic openness to Being. It is not irrational frenzy but heightened attunement. Latin inspiratus spiritualizes it. Heidegger’s Begeisterung (in‑spiritedness) captures the existential dimension.

80
ἔπος (epos)
verbum
Wort
word / utterance
ἔπος means a spoken word or utterance, often in epic poetry. Heidegger uses it to explore the primordial power of language. It is not a linguistic unit but a revealing event. Latin verbum reduces it to a grammatical term. Heidegger’s Wort is ontological.

81
ἔριον (erion)
lana
Wolle
wool / thread (cosmic weaving)
Reiterated here with a cosmological nuance: early Greek cosmology often uses weaving metaphors. Heidegger sees weaving as a metaphor for the interlacing of presencing and absencing. The cosmos is woven, not constructed. Latin lana loses the metaphysical resonance.

82
ἔρως (erōs)
amor
Liebe
desire / longing
ἔρως is the primordial longing that draws beings together. Heidegger interprets it as the pull of Being itself. It is not merely erotic desire but ontological attraction. Latin amor narrows it to emotional love. Heidegger’s Liebe is existential.

83
ἔστιν (estin)
est
ist
is / there is
The simple verb “is” becomes the central question of Western metaphysics. For Parmenides, “ἐστίν” names the self‑showing of Being. Heidegger reopens the question of the “is” as the forgotten foundation of ontology. Latin est becomes a logical copula. Heidegger’s ist is phenomenological.

84
ἦμαρ (ēmar)
dies
Tag
day
ἦμαρ means day, but for the Greeks it also signifies the realm of light and presence. Heidegger interprets it as the temporal clearing in which beings appear. It is not a unit of time but a mode of presencing. Latin dies loses the ontological depth.

85
ἦχος (ēchos)
sonus
Klang
sound / resonance
ἦχος means sound or echo. Heidegger uses resonance as a metaphor for how Being “resounds” in language. It is not mere auditory vibration but ontological reverberation. Latin sonus reduces it to physical sound. Heidegger’s Klang preserves the metaphysical sense.

86
θεῖον (theion)
divinum
das Göttliche
the divine
θεῖον refers to the divine as a quality, not a personal god. Heidegger interprets it as the dimension of the holy that precedes theology. It is the region where Being reveals itself as sacred. Latin divinum shifts toward metaphysical substance. Heidegger’s das Göttliche is existential.

87
θεός (theos)
deus
Gott
god
θεός originally means “the one who runs” or “the one who shines.” Heidegger interprets gods as modes of world‑disclosure. They are not supernatural beings but manifestations of Being. Latin deus becomes a metaphysical entity. Heidegger’s Gott is phenomenological.

88
θνητός (thnētos)
mortalis
sterblich
mortal
θνητός means mortal, capable of death. Heidegger emphasizes mortality as the defining feature of human existence. Mortality opens the human to Being. Latin mortalis is biological. Heidegger’s sterblich is existential.

89
ἱερόν (hieron)
sacrum
das Heilige
the holy
ἱερόν means holy or sacred. Heidegger interprets it as the region where Being reveals itself as worthy of reverence. It is not religious sanctity but ontological holiness. Latin sacrum narrows it. Heidegger’s das Heilige is foundational for his later thought.

90
ἱστορία (historia)
historia
Geschichte
inquiry / history
ἱστορία originally means inquiry or investigation. Heidegger retrieves this sense to critique modern historiography. True history (Geschichte) is the happening of Being. Latin historia becomes narrative history. Heidegger’s Geschichte is ontological.

91
κάλλος (kallos)
pulchritudo
Schönheit
beauty
κάλλος means beauty as radiant presence. Heidegger interprets beauty as a mode of truth’s happening. It is not aesthetic pleasure but ontological shining. Latin pulchritudo aestheticizes it. Heidegger’s Schönheit is tied to unconcealment.

92
κλέος (kleos)
gloria
Ruhm
glory / renown
κλέος means glory or fame, literally “what is heard.” Heidegger interprets it as the way a human being’s Being resounds in the world. It is not vanity but existential presence. Latin gloria moralizes it. Heidegger’s Ruhm is ontological.

93
κόσμος (kosmos)
mundus
Welt
world / order
Reiterated here to emphasize its centrality. κόσμος is the ordered whole of beings. Heidegger interprets it as world, the open region where beings appear. Latin mundus shifts toward physical universe. Heidegger’s Welt is existential.

94
κρύπτεσθαι (kryptesthai)
occultari
sich verbergen
to conceal / to hide
κρύπτεσθαι means to hide or conceal. Heidegger interprets it as the withdrawal of Being. Concealment is not negation but a necessary part of truth. Latin occultari mystifies it. Heidegger’s sich verbergen is structural.

95
λόγος (logos)
ratio
Rede
gathering / saying
Reiterated here to emphasize its foundational role. λόγος is the gathering that lets beings appear. Heidegger interprets it as the structural articulation of Being. Latin ratio narrows it to reason. Heidegger’s Rede is existential.

96
μέλος (melos)
carmen
Lied
song / measure
μέλος means song or melody. Heidegger uses it to describe the rhythmic unfolding of Being. It is not entertainment but ontological measure. Latin carmen poeticizes it. Heidegger’s Lied is existential.

97
μνήμη (mnēmē)
memoria
Erinnerung
memory / recollection
μνήμη means memory as recollection of what is present. Heidegger interprets it as the capacity to hold Being in mind. It is not psychological recall but ontological remembrance. Latin memoria narrows it. Heidegger’s Erinnerung is tied to thinking.

98
μοῖρα (moira)
fatum
Geschick
destiny / allotment
Reiterated here to emphasize its role in Heidegger’s thought. μοῖρα is the allotment given to each being. Heidegger interprets it as the sending (Geschick) of Being. It is not fatalism but ontological distribution. Latin fatum distorts it.

99
νύξ (nyx)
nox
Nacht
night
νύξ means night, the realm of concealment. Heidegger interprets night as the withdrawal of Being. It is not mere darkness but the hiddenness that makes unconcealment possible. Latin nox loses the ontological nuance. Heidegger’s Nacht is metaphysical.

100
ξένος (xenos)
hospes
Fremder
stranger / foreigner
ξένος means stranger or guest. Heidegger interprets the stranger as the one who stands outside the familiar clearing. The stranger reveals the limits of one’s world. Latin hospes conflates guest and host. Heidegger’s Fremder is existential.
